Post 1: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats alignment as learning which of two completions is preferred, avoiding the conventional RLHF sequence of fitting a reward model and then running reinforcement learning against it. [shard_01335_36211] [shard_02738_62757]  
For prompt \(x\), preferred completion \(y_w\), rejected completion \(y_l\), trainable policy \(\pi_\theta\), reference policy \(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\), and temperature \(\beta\), DPO minimizes \(-\log\sigma\{\beta[(\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w|x))-(\log\pi_\theta(y_l|x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l|x))]\}\), so optimization raises the winner’s log-likelihood ratio relative to the loser’s while retaining a reference-policy anchor. [shard_02738_62757]  
This objective follows by writing the KL-regularized optimal reward as \(r(x,y)=\beta\log[\pi_r(y|x)/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)]+\beta\log Z(x)\), substituting it into the Bradley–Terry preference probability, and observing that the unknown prompt-dependent partition term \(Z(x)\) cancels between compared answers. [shard_02738_62757]  
DPO is attractive for dialogue, summarization, sentiment control, and other offline preference datasets because it uses a classification-style loss rather than online sampling and has matched or improved upon PPO-based RLHF in reported evaluations. [shard_01335_36211]  
Its unresolved problem is not merely optimizer choice: preference labels can be expensive, inconsistent, and too weak to judge outputs beyond human expertise, while both preference-trained policies and their evaluators can fail under distribution shift or adversarial jailbreaks. [shard_02325_38369]  

Post 2: QLoRA makes adaptation feasible when the practical bottleneck is memory rather than the absence of a useful base model, by freezing a quantized backbone and learning only small low-rank updates. [shard_03037_43578] [shard_03811_12630]  
For a frozen weight matrix \(W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}\), LoRA replaces \(W_0x\) with \(W_0x+(\alpha/r)BAx\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{in}}}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times r}\), and \(r\ll\min(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}})\), reducing trainable parameters from \(d_{\text{out}}d_{\text{in}}\) to \(r(d_{\text{out}}+d_{\text{in}})\). [shard_03811_12630]  
QLoRA stores \(W_0\) in four-bit NormalFloat form, uses blockwise quantization and quantizes the block-scale constants again through double quantization, then dequantizes for BF16 gradient computation while keeping the adapter matrices trainable. [shard_03811_12630]  
Paged optimizers spill optimizer state to CPU memory during sequence-length-driven GPU-memory spikes, completing a design intended to enable single-GPU fine-tuning of models as large as 65 billion parameters. [shard_03037_43578] [shard_03811_12630]  
The technique is well suited to domain instruction tuning and rapid experimentation under limited hardware, but rank selection, quantization error, sequence-length peaks, and the possibility that a low-rank update cannot express a difficult behavioral change remain engineering and modeling constraints. [shard_03811_12630]  

Post 3: Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning (RAFT) addresses the mismatch between generic instruction tuning and a domain-specific “open-book” deployment, where the model must answer from retrieved enterprise, biomedical, news, or code documents despite imperfect retrieval. [shard_03282_73788]  
Each RAFT example contains a question \(Q\), \(k\) documents, and a chain-of-thought-style target answer \(A^\ast\), with an oracle document \(D^\ast\) retained alongside distractors for a fraction \(P\) of examples and omitted for the remaining \(1-P\) examples. [shard_03282_73788]  
Standard supervised next-token training on this mixture simultaneously teaches the model to quote and reason from relevant evidence when it is available and to retain useful in-domain knowledge when retrieval supplies only distractors. [shard_03282_73788]  
This is especially useful for a private-document question-answering system whose test domain is known in advance, and reported evaluations cover PubMedQA, HotpotQA, and API-documentation tasks. [shard_02849_58209] [shard_03282_73788]  
RAFT does not repair a badly maintained corpus or guarantee grounded answers, because its success still depends on domain coverage, generated or curated question–answer supervision, retrieval conditions resembling training, and careful handling of distractors. [shard_03282_73788]  

Post 4: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) targets reasoning settings with verifiable or scoreable outcomes, seeking PPO-style improvement without training a separate critic or value model. [shard_01751_80083] [shard_05381_75364]  
For \(G\) sampled completions of one prompt with rewards \(r_1,\ldots,r_G\), GRPO assigns each token of completion \(i\) the group-relative advantage \(\hat A_{i,t}=(r_i-\operatorname{mean}(r))/\operatorname{std}(r)\), so above-average sampled solutions are reinforced and below-average ones are suppressed. [shard_05381_75364]  
The resulting clipped policy-gradient update retains PPO’s conservative likelihood-ratio logic but uses within-group relative reward as the baseline, trading critic memory and training cost for multiple samples per prompt. [shard_01751_80083] [shard_05381_75364]  
Math reasoning is a natural use case because final answers can often be checked automatically, and process supervision can additionally score intermediate reasoning steps rather than only the terminal answer. [shard_01751_80083] [shard_05381_75364]  
Its central open challenge is reward validity: group normalization only ranks samples relative to one another, so a flawed outcome verifier or process reward can systematically reinforce superficially convincing but incorrect reasoning. [shard_05381_75364]
